title: The Art of AI Monks
description: The Art of AI Monks traces the virtual monk’s prehistory, five researched profiles, 66 unverified Instagram leads, short-video structures, and the paths from feeds to books and products.
markdown:
# The Art of AI Monks

*One feed offers a quiet reflection. The next promises an old remedy. A robe can point to a real teacher, a synthetic persona, or a product page—and those are different stories.*

There is no ordination committee in the scroll. One clip offers a few words for a hard day. Another, described by an investigation, puts cabbage in a sock. A profile can lead to a book, a wellness product, or a comment-to-message exchange. The monk-like image is easy to recognize. The business and the person behind it take more work to identify.

“AI monk” is not one category. It can describe a synthetic persona, an account that an investigation classifies as AI-generated, or a real monk speaking through a digital character. Some profiles remain unresolved. Calling every robe an AI avatar would make a neat headline and a bad database.

## What counts as an AI monk?

For this guide, an AI monk avatar is a monk-like persona in social video with evidence that the person or performance is AI-generated or labeled as AI. A robe, temple backdrop, or old face alone does not establish that.

Three cases can look alike on a phone: a synthetic persona, a real religious teacher using an animated character, and an account whose origin has not been established. The distinction is the story. If we flatten all three into one trend, we miss the creator, the audience promise, and the commercial route.

## Read the evidence before the face

A directory needs labels that describe where a claim comes from. **Confirmed** means a creator, platform, or credible report identifies a synthetic persona. **Reported** preserves an investigation’s classification when identity details are incomplete or another source disagrees. **Unverified** means a screenshot or name has not been independently checked.

[Maldita’s July 2026 investigation](https://maldita.es/investigaciones/20260727/250-ai-health-instagram-accounts/) collected 250 AI-generated health profiles. It reported more than 45,600 posts, over 53.7 million followers, and at least seven languages: English, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, German, and Russian. Its team says it found profiles in feeds and among the followers of accounts it had already collected, then checked account details, links, Meta AI labels, watermarks, and visible signs of synthetic media. It says 61.2% of the profiles posted in English and 52.8% had the United States as the platform-reported country signal; that field does not establish an operator's residence.

This is a broad health-account sample, not a monk census. The report placed 82 profiles in an “ancestral wisdom” group that includes monks and other people portrayed through racialized stereotypes. It found 224 accounts with visible product URLs; more than half linked to external websites, often for supplements, and 30.8% promoted books or PDFs. The same report counted 13 religious/preacher profiles, including non-Buddhist figures such as nuns, priests, and Amish-style characters. Those percentages describe all 250 health profiles, not the monk subset.

A separate [Maldita report on 16 Instagram and Facebook profiles](https://maldita.es/investigaciones/20260710/cuentas-ia-instagram-facebook-salud-libros/) reported 3.5 million followers and more than 70.5 million views across the most-viewed clips it examined. It names Shaolin-style profiles Leo Chen and SifuChen California. Those are reported audience and view totals, not evidence of paid orders.

## The virtual monk came before the AI influencer

[Thai PBS profiled Phra Maha AI](https://www.thaipbsworld.com/around-thailand/thailands-first-virtual-monk-to-preach-buddhism-to-new-generation), a real Thai monk who worked with programmers on a 2D animated character to share Buddhist teachings with younger people. It is an earlier virtual presentation of a real monk, not proof that the monk himself was generated by AI.

A screenshot supplied for this research shows that Yang Mun’s YouTube channel joined on 4 November 2025. That is a channel date, not the character’s creation date. The public sources reviewed here do not establish the first AI monk avatar across every language and platform. A first-place claim would need a broader, dated search than this one.

## Five profiles, five different routes into the story

### Yang Mun — a large audience, and a disputed identity

[HeyGen](https://www.heygen.com/customer-stories/yangmun) and Columbia identify Shalev Hani as the creator of an AI character. A [first-party page linked by Columbia](https://www.yangmuns.com/blog/the-truth-behind-%E2%80%9Ctime-to-heal%E2%80%9D-by-yang-mun) says the teacher is real and only the voice is AI-translated. The sources disagree, so the index marks the AI status as reported and keeps the conflict visible. The public Instagram is [@yangmunus](https://www.instagram.com/yangmunus/); the YouTube channel is [@Yangmunv2](https://www.youtube.com/@Yangmunv2). Its sales page lists a $49.99 Journey and a $59.99 bundle with three eBooks. The exact TikTok handles remain unknown.

### Ming San — a report calls it AI; another profile leaves the question open

Maldita includes [@mingsanhealing](https://www.instagram.com/mingsanhealing/) in its AI-generated health-profile investigation. Its 20–21 July snapshot showed about 1.2 million followers and a cabbage-in-socks video at 2.2 million views. A screenshot supplied for this index shows 1.37 million followers, but has no capture date. The profile links to a beetroot product; the link does not reveal commission or sales. AvatarFactory’s [Ming San profile](https://avatarfactory.io/ai-influencers/ming-san) says the public evidence does not establish whether the persona is AI. The index preserves both descriptions.

### SifuChen California — a guide behind a story highlight

Maldita describes a Shaolin-style profile that routes viewers from a highlighted story to a €16.45 guide, “130 Natural Remedies of the Shaolin Temple.” The report says the profile displayed a Spanish flag. That is a profile signal, not proof of the operator’s location or of every post’s language. The live handle is unresolved, so the record links an [archived profile](https://archive.li/CZww4) instead of guessing one.

### Leo Chen — a comment can lead to a book

Maldita reports that a Leo Chen video had more than 2.2 million views at its observation and asked viewers to comment for a “Chinese Natural Healing” book or PDF. The report notes visual signs it considered AI-generated. The exact account handle, price, and paid conversion are unknown. A comment can collect interest; it cannot prove a purchase.

### Yan Chen / monjechen — Spanish text, an AI label, and a cropped link

A supplied screen shows [@monjechen](https://www.instagram.com/monjechen/), Spanish-language profile text, an “AI-generated profile” label, and a product link cut off at the edge. It also shows 1.34 million followers and 584 posts, without a capture date. The label has not been independently read back and the destination is unknown, so its AI status remains unverified. Similar names are not enough to merge it with another account.

The five records do not share one certainty level. A public claim, an investigative classification, and a screenshot clue carry different weight. Follower counts, views, seller prices, paid orders, and profit are different measures too.

## A short video is a tiny story, not a universal script

Yang Mun’s 65-second “Words of Motivation” keeps one centered shot: robe, book, candlelight, direct eye contact. It offers reassurance, connects it to ordinary hopes, and ends with a morning-and-night reflection. There is no visible paid pitch in this sample.

[youtube-short:Er2Ig4GM7z0|Words of Motivation from Yang Mun]

Other clips start with a problem, a surprising prop, or an urgent health claim. The Maldita reports describe videos about remedies and comments that request a book. Captions keep the point legible without sound. A profile link, a highlighted story, or a comment keyword can offer the next step.

The recurring structure is not one shared sentence. It is a recognizable presenter, one question, a quick turn, and an action that can happen after the video. Yang Mun’s calm reflection, Leo Chen’s comment-to-message route, and SifuChen’s highlight link ask the viewer to do different things. Public examples do not prove that every account uses the same tool or script.

## A book, a supplement, and a program are different offers

Yang Mun’s own checkout page sells a 30-day program and an eBook bundle. SifuChen’s reported path leads to a guide. Leo Chen’s reported prompt begins with a comment. Ming San’s screenshot shows an external wellness-product link. Each route needs its own record: what the page offers, where it sends the viewer, and which parts remain unknown.

The percentages from Maldita’s 250-profile investigation belong to the full health sample. They show that external sites, supplements, books, and PDFs appear in the broader ecosystem. They cannot be presented as monk-avatar conversion rates. A link is not an order, and an affiliate destination does not reveal a commission.

For an eBook seller, the important steps are visible: attract attention with a video, build recognition, move interested viewers to a profile, then present a product with a clear promise. To learn whether the route works, measure profile visits, link taps, purchases, refunds, fees, and net revenue separately. Public follower counts alone will not answer the business question.

## The AI video factory is a claim to verify, not a magic recipe

HeyGen’s customer story says Hani moved from a few videos per week to daily publishing, calls the cadence seven times higher, and estimates about 20 minutes of production per video. These are figures in a vendor case study, not an independently audited production log.

A separate [GrowwStacks walkthrough](https://growwstacks.com/blog/ai-factory-creates-ai-avatar-instagram-videos-daily-n8n-automation) describes an Airtable-to-LLM-to-HeyGen workflow followed by captions and posting. It claims savings of more than 20 hours per month. That is the vendor’s claim, not confirmation of Yang Mun’s internal system.

A useful open-source pipeline can still be built around the observable work: find a candidate, verify the public identity, capture the source and date, describe the clip’s structure in original words, write a fresh script, disclose synthetic media, publish, and track what happens after the link. The process is teachable without copying someone else’s face, voice, script, or design.

## A robe can carry trust before the viewer hears a claim

A real monk using an animated character, a disclosed fictional persona, and an account with an unclear origin can look alike in a vertical video. They do not make the same promise to the viewer.

For Buddhists, robes and temple settings carry meaning beyond their color palette. A creator should explain who is speaking, what tradition informs the message, and whether a health claim has evidence behind it. That clarity lets people enjoy a strange corner of internet culture without mistaking a costume for credentials.

## The index now connects nine researched profiles and 66 discovery leads

The [AI Monk Index](https://aniccaai.com/ai-monk-database) has nine researched profile records and 66 Instagram leads transcribed from supplied screenshots. The leads are explicitly unverified: AI origin, operators, languages and offers remain unresolved for many leads; dated public counts are added only when a source was actually read. They are not 66 confirmed AI monks, and the index is not a census.

Search the directory by name, language, platform, or evidence status, then open the source for each researched record. The [open dataset](https://aniccaai.com/data/ai-monk-avatar-database-2026.json) keeps the unknowns beside the findings so other researchers can help check them. This archive is a starting shelf for a future book about AI monks, not a claim that the whole monastery has been counted.

## The open index keeps growing

The five-profile study above is the starting sample, not the whole market. The [live AI Monk Index](https://aniccaai.com/ai-monk-database) now contains 75 records: 9 researched profiles and 66 discovery leads, with 48 source references. The new English-first research adds Kai Tsukimi, Yangjun and Buddha Would Say; a Master Kaizen TikTok candidate remains unclassified by language. Their AI origins remain unverified. Dated public audiences and seller-listed products help prioritize further research; they do not prove paid orders or profit.
